**It fails safe.** With a settings override, a misconfiguration or a hostile repo means you silently use *someone else's* catalog. Without it, the worst case is you use *ours*. For a default, that's the right direction.

**It drops two settings loads per sync.** `resolvePluginIndexURL` wouldn't need to touch settings at all — a cost the architecture review flagged separately.

## The one thing you lose, stated honestly

The feature and the vulnerability are the same mechanism. The value of committed `index_url` is that a contributor who clones the repo gets a different catalog **without knowing**. That's the vulnerability described as a feature. You can't keep one and drop the other — you can only choose whether the redirect is *visible* (my Option B) or *impossible* (yours).

For the internal-catalog use case, `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` in a shell profile or onboarding doc still works, and works across all repos rather than per-repo — arguably better for a company-wide catalog.

There's a useful precedent here that's worth putting in the Thomas message: **Go has no repo-committed way to redirect `GOPROXY`** — it's env or user-level `go env -w`. **npm does allow a per-project `.npmrc` with `registry=`, and it's a well-known supply-chain footgun.** The stricter choice has better company.

## One variant worth knowing about

You could allow `settings.local.json` (gitignored, so not attacker-controlled) while rejecting the committed `settings.json`. That gives a dev a persistent per-repo override without the drive-by.

I'd skip it. The settings package doesn't currently thread file provenance through the merge, so it's real work, and the env var already covers persistence. Only worth it if someone specifically wants per-repo-but-not-committed.

Drop `plugins.index_url` entirely, keep `--index` and the env var, and cut `index_ttl_hours` at the same time so the whole struct goes. That resolves bucket 2 and one of the four bucket-3 cuts in a single change, and it's strictly less code than the branch has today.

Take the plugin index URL out of repo-committed settings

plugins.index_url was read from .entire/settings.json — a committed file
resolved from the working directory — while an index-listed repository installs
with no confirmation prompt. Composed, that meant cloning a repo containing four
lines of JSON and running `entire plugin install <any-name-in-their-catalog>`
downloaded an attacker-chosen binary, chmod 0755, and linked it onto the user's
PATH with no prompt, no --yes, and no warning. `plugin browse` did it on one
keypress.

The setting cannot be kept and made safe. Its whole value was that contributors
got a different catalog *without knowing* — that is the vulnerability stated as
a feature. The options were to make the redirect visible (prompt per unseen
index) or impossible; this takes the second, because it deletes code instead of
adding trust state, and because it fails safe: a missing override now falls back
to the curated default rather than to someone else's catalog.

Organizations wanting an internal catalog set ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL, which
applies across repositories rather than per-repository and cannot be chosen by
content the user merely checked out. Go takes the same position — nothing
committed can redirect GOPROXY — and npm's per-project registry override is the
cautionary counter-example.

plugins.index_ttl_hours goes with it: `plugin index update` already forces a
refresh and stale-on-offline already covers a failed one, so the knob tuned a
problem solved twice while costing a settings load per sync. The TTL is now a
fixed 24h constant.

Between them the whole PluginSettings struct, its validator, its merge path and
its tests are gone — 320 lines, and the plugin layer now reads no settings at
all, so resolvePluginIndexURL no longer needs a context. The URL validator moves
back to the cli package as the single definition, which is where its only
remaining callers live.

A deprecated, ignored Plugins field is retained for one reason: without it a
settings file left over from when the keys existed fails the strict loader, and
that breaks every command that loads settings — `entire status` included — with
an opaque "unknown field" error. Same tolerance the removed Strategy key gets.

ParsePluginMetadata used strict decoding, the exact inverse of the choice made
for index.json in this same branch — where the reasoning is that an artifact
read by every shipped CLI version must degrade rather than refuse.

entire-plugin.yml is that same class of artifact and has no version field to
gate on, so the first plugin author to adopt any future field (min_cli_version,
bin_name, …) would break installs on every older CLI, permanently, with no way
to fix it for those users.

The trade is asymmetric in the other direction too: strict decoding caught
author typos, which costs the author one confused test run against their own
plugin. A forward-compatibility break is unfixable and fleet-wide.
Author-side validation belongs in a lint command, not in the path every user's
install runs through.

Timing is why this goes in now rather than later: once third-party
entire-plugin.yml files exist, older CLIs stay broken forever.

content.text:
All 11 GitHub checks pass. Entire Gates is still running its fresh agent review.

## Done — `600eae5c6` and `9c1de62dd`

**1. Index URL out of repo-committed settings**

`plugins.index_url` and `plugins.index_ttl_hours` are gone, and with them the whole `PluginSettings` struct, its validator, its merge path, and its 162-line test file — **320 lines deleted**. The plugin layer now reads no settings at all, so `resolvePluginIndexURL` doesn't even need a context. The URL validator moved back into `cli` as the single definition, since that's where its only remaining callers live.

Net effect on the settings package versus main: **+39 lines** (a deprecated field and one test), down from +320. The `settings.go` merge-conflict surface with main is effectively gone.

Verified by smoke test — a repo committing `{"plugins":{"index_url":"https://evil.example/idx"}}` now gets the real curated index:

```
$ entire plugin search        # run from inside that repo
  run       Launch one of the agents enabled for Entire...
  upgrade   Upgrade the system-installed Entire binary [official]
```

**2. Lenient `entire-plugin.yml` decoding** — the deadline-sensitive one. The test now pins that a file carrying an unknown field still parses *and* keeps its known fields, so a future `min_cli_version` can't break older CLIs.

## One thing I found and handled that you should know about

Removing the settings keys made a leftover `plugins` key **hard-fail the strict loader**, which broke `entire status` — not just plugin commands — with an opaque `unknown field "plugins"`. Anyone who tried the feature during development would hit that, plausibly including Thomas, since the PR body says he validated against production.

I followed the repo's existing precedent (the deprecated `Strategy` key) and kept a tolerated, ignored `Plugins map[string]any` field. Confirmed end-to-end:

```
$ entire status               # with a leftover plugins key
● Enabled · branch main
```

This is the one piece of the change I made a judgment call on without asking — it's three lines, it matches an established pattern, and the alternative was shipping a change that bricks an unrelated command for early adopters.

## What this means for the Thomas brief

Bucket 2 is now resolved in code rather than described, and one of the four bucket-3 cuts came along with it. Worth updating the message you copied: instead of "here's a vulnerability and four fix options," it's now "here's the fix, 320 lines net deletion, CI green" — with the design question for him being whether he accepts losing committed internal catalogs in favor of `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL`.

Still open from bucket 3: `requires[]` (the big one), `browse`, and `platforms`. Those are genuine scope decisions on his PR, and I'd leave them to him.

And still open, unrelated to either bucket: the name-reconciliation defect at `plugin_deps.go:251` — the installed plugin name comes from the remote rather than what was requested. Three independent reviewers found it and it's the only open trail finding. It's a real bug rather than a design question, so if you want it fixed I can take it; it just wasn't in the buckets we scoped.
This whole PR is not merged so I think it's fine to just ignore this and keep hard failing

Agreed, and there's a better reason than "it's unmerged."

My `Strategy` precedent was weaker than I implied: that field tolerates config that **actually shipped**. `plugins.index_url` never did. And tolerate-and-ignore has a real downside I underweighted — a company that took the PR's advice and committed `plugins.index_url` would silently get the *public* catalog while believing their internal one was configured. For a security-relevant redirect, failing loudly is better than failing quietly.

Done. The tolerance field is gone, and a High-severity finding on my own code surfaced and got fixed in the same pass.

## Your call was right, plus a better reason

Removed `Plugins map[string]any` and its test — `ac51853c6`. The settings package is now **byte-identical to main**: the plugin layer adds no schema at all.

Beyond "it's unmerged," the argument I'd actually put in the commit: tolerate-and-ignore was worse for the one case that mattered. The removed setting existed so a company could commit an internal catalog — silently ignoring it would leave such a repo on the *public* index while its authors believed otherwise. `unknown field "plugins"` forces the migration to `ENTIRE_PLUGIN_INDEX_URL` to be noticed. And my `Strategy` precedent was weaker than I made it sound: that field tolerates config that actually shipped.

## The High finding — my own bug

Entire Gates flagged a credential leak at `plugin_fetch.go`, and it was legitimate: my earlier commit said *"Credentials no longer reach logs, output, or disk"* and that was **false**. I covered the four git paths and missed the HTTP one.

`releaseAssetBaseURL` derives the asset URL from the repo URL, and `url.String()` re-serializes embedded userinfo — so `REDACTED` yields a credentialed download URL, which thirteen error paths then interpolated verbatim. `main.go` prints command errors straight to stderr, so any ordinary failure — unreachable host, 5xx, checksum mismatch, oversize — printed the token to a terminal or CI log.

Fixed in `ba64c9c5f`, with a regression test across five failure modes, verified RED first:

```
case 0 leaked the credential: download REDACTED
  : Get "REDACTED" : dial tcp: no such host
```

That output is worth a second look — Go had **already** masked its own nested error to `bob:***@host`. The leak was entirely our wrapper around it. Which is why the test asserts on the full error string rather than trusting the transport layer to sanitize, and why I'd distrust any similar claim elsewhere in the codebase that hasn't been tested this way.

```
PR #1422 · head ba64c9c5f · out of draft · MERGEABLE
14 commits ahead of main · all GitHub checks green · lint 0 issues
Trail #973 — High finding resolved
```

Two things outstanding, both genuine decisions rather than defects:

- **`plugin_deps.go:251`** — still the one open finding: the installed plugin name comes from the remote rather than what was requested, so a dependency can install under a different name and be reported missing forever. Found by three independent reviewers now. It's a real bug, not a design question — say the word and I'll fix it.
- **Bucket 3 remainder** — `requires[]`, `browse`, `platforms`. Thomas's scope calls.

For the brief you copied: bucket 2 is now resolved in code, not described. The framing shifts from "here's a vulnerability and four options" to "here's the fix, 320 lines net deletion, settings package back to identical-with-main" — with the one question for Thomas being whether he accepts losing committed internal catalogs in favor of the env var.

add="""#### The installed name must match what was requested

The installed plugin name comes from the *remote* — `entire-plugin.yml`'s `name:`, else the repository basename. Whenever the caller has already committed to a name, that name is passed down as `ExpectedName` and a mismatch is fatal. Three paths set it: an index-resolved install (the catalog entry the user typed), a dependency install (the requirement being satisfied), and an upgrade (the plugin being upgraded).
